Surprisingly, we find that this may not work for numerical commonsense knowledge (e.g., a bird usually has two legs). In this paper, we investigate whether and to what extent we can induce numerical commonsense knowledge from PTLMs as well as the robustness of this process. To study this, we introduce a novel probing task with a diagnostic dataset, NumerSense, containing 13.6k masked-word-prediction probes (10.5k for fine-tuning and 3.1k for testing). Our analysis reveals that: (1) BERT and its stronger variant RoBERTa perform poorly on the diagnostic dataset prior to any fine-tuning; (2) fine-tuning with distant supervision brings some improvement; (3) the best supervised model still performs poorly as compared to human performance (54.06% vs 96.3% in accuracy).

papers.title: Hypothesis Testing the Circuit Hypothesis in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the circuit hypothesis in large language models, which posits that capabilities are implemented by small subnetworks (circuits)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes criteria for circuits in LLMs and develops a suite of hypothesis tests to evaluate how well circuits satisfy these criteria, along with an empirical study of existing circuits.
papers.conclusion: The hypothesis testing framework provides a rigorous way to evaluate circuits, and the empirical study shows that existing circuits partially align with the circuit hypothesis, with room for improvement.
papers.key_findings:
Synthetic circuits (Tracr) align well with the idealized circuit properties.
Discovered circuits (e.g., Induction, IOI, Docstring) vary in how well they meet the idealized criteria, with Induction passing two tests and Docstring passing one.
The hypothesis tests can identify unnecessary edges in circuits, showing that some circuits can be improved.
papers.limitation:
The hypothesis testing framework may be susceptible to p-hacking if misused.
The tests assume a fixed experimental setup and may not generalize across different setups.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate surprising capabilities, but we do not understand how they are implemented. One hypothesis suggests that these capabilities are primarily executed by small subnetworks within the LLM, known as circuits. But how can we evaluate this hypothesis? In this paper, we formalize a set of criteria that a circuit is hypothesized to meet and develop a suite of hypothesis tests to evaluate how well circuits satisfy them. The criteria focus on the extent to which the LLM's behavior is preserved, the degree of localization of this behavior, and whether the circuit is minimal. We apply these tests to six circuits described in the research literature. We find that synthetic circuits -- circuits that are hard-coded in the model -- align with the idealized properties. Circuits discovered in Transformer models satisfy the criteria to varying degrees. To facilitate future empirical studies of circuits, we created the \textit{circuitry} package, a wrapper around the \textit{TransformerLens} library, which abstracts away lower-level manipulations of hooks and activations. The software is available at \url{https://github.com/blei-lab/circuitry}.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: Uncovering Intermediate Variables in Transformers using Circuit Probing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically uncover low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit probing, a method that combines probing and causal analysis to automatically uncover circuits computing hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Circuit probing provides a unified approach for a variety of analyses, combining and extending the capabilities of existing methods for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit probing can decipher the algorithms learned by models on simple arithmetic tasks.
Circuit probing reveals modular structure within a model, showing that shared and free variables are computed by distinct circuits.
Circuit probing tracks the development of circuits over training, showing circuit formation occurs continuously before generalization.
Circuit probing uncovers circuits responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.
Circuit probing is more faithful to the underlying model computation than linear probing, nonlinear probing, and amnesic probing.
papers.limitation: Neurons are typically polysemantic, so the assumption that a circuit is only causally implicated in computing a single intermediate variable may not hold completely.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have achieved high performance on a wide variety of complex tasks, but the algorithms that they implement are notoriously difficult to interpret. It is often necessary to hypothesize intermediate variables involved in a network's computation in order to understand these algorithms. For example, does a language model depend on particular syntactic properties when generating a sentence? Yet, existing analysis tools make it difficult to test hypotheses of this type. We propose a new analysis technique - circuit probing - that automatically uncovers low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables. This enables causal analysis through targeted ablation at the level of model parameters. We apply this method to models trained on simple arithmetic tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness at (1) deciphering the algorithms that models have learned, (2) revealing modular structure within a model, and (3) tracking the development of circuits over training. Across these three experiments we demonstrate that circuit probing combines and extends the capabilities of existing methods, providing one unified approach for a variety of analyses. Finally, we demonstrate circuit probing on a real-world use case: uncovering circuits that are responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.

papers.title: Through a Compressed Lens: Investigating The Impact of Quantization on Factual Knowledge Recall
papers.research_question: How does quantization affect factual knowledge recall (FKR) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Quantization typically leads to information loss and degrades factual knowledge recall, especially in smaller models, but BitSandBytes is most effective at preserving FKR and quantization remains a viable compression strategy.
papers.conclusion: Quantization generally leads to information loss and factual knowledge recall degradation, but effects vary by model and technique, and it remains a viable compression strategy.
papers.key_findings:
Quantization typically impairs factual knowledge recall, with more pronounced effects in smaller models within a family.
Models quantized to lower bit precision do not consistently underperform higher-precision versions.
Quantization can occasionally improve factual knowledge recall, possibly due to regularization or noise effects.
BitSandBytes (BITSANDBYTES) quantization best preserves the original model's factual knowledge recall capability.
No observed performance degradation is severe enough to compromise quantization as an effective compression strategy.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are confined to English-language datasets.
Experiments are restricted to Llama3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B due to computational constraints.
The study is limited to post-training quantization techniques and does not include lower-bit quantization (e.g., 1-bit or 2-bit) or weight-activation quantization.
future_direction: Extending experiments to multilingual settings.
Investigating the impact of lower-bit quantization (e.g., 1-bit or 2-bit).
Studying the impact of weight-activation quantization, KV cache compression, or quantization-aware training techniques on factual knowledge recall.
papers.abstract: Quantization methods are widely used to accelerate inference and streamline the deployment of large language models (LLMs). Although quantization's effects on various LLM capabilities have been extensively studied, one critical area remains underexplored: factual knowledge recall (FKR), the process by which LLMs access stored knowledge. To this end, we conduct comprehensive experiments using three common quantization techniques at distinct bit widths, in conjunction with interpretability-driven analyses on two tasks, knowledge memorization and latent multi-hop reasoning. We show that quantization typically results in information loss within LLMs, consequently diminishing their capacity for FKR. This effect is particularly amplified in smaller models within the same architectural families. However, models quantized at reduced bit precision do not consistently exhibit inferior performance and occasionally quantization may even enhance model FKR. We find that BitSandBytes demonstrates highest preservation of the original full-precision model's FKR. Despite variability across models and methods, quantization causes modest performance degradation and remains an effective compression strategy.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire factual knowledge during training, and what are the dynamics, the impact of data distribution, and the challenges of integrating new knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-phase learning process for factual recall in language models, shows how data distribution affects dynamics, and demonstrates that fine-tuning to add new knowledge is challenging due to hallucinations and corruption of existing memories.
papers.conclusion: The paper emphasizes the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggests data scheduling strategies to accelerate training, while highlighting the difficulty of integrating new knowledge post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn factual recall in three phases: initial language understanding, a performance plateau, and then knowledge emergence.
The plateau phase corresponds to the development of attention-based recall circuits.
Imbalanced data distributions shorten the plateau but can lead to overfitting.
Hallucinations (overconfident predictions on unseen individuals) emerge simultaneously with knowledge acquisition.
Fine-tuning to incorporate new knowledge quickly corrupts existing parametric memories.
papers.limitation: The results do not rule out that other qualitative changes may occur during the plateau phase, and they do not provide any mechanistic insights regarding how models acquire individual-specific knowledge.
future_direction: Further investigation is needed to better understand the precise conditions under which data repetition can effectively reduce time spent on performance plateaus during training.
The data scheduling strategy could be dynamically adjusted based on observed plateau termination.
papers.abstract: Large language models accumulate vast knowledge during pre-training, yet the dynamics governing this acquisition remain poorly understood. This work investigates the learning dynamics of language models on a synthetic factual recall task, uncovering three key findings: First, language models learn in three phases, exhibiting a performance plateau before acquiring precise factual knowledge. Mechanistically, this plateau coincides with the formation of attention-based circuits that support recall. Second, the training data distribution significantly impacts learning dynamics, as imbalanced distributions lead to shorter plateaus. Finally, hallucinations emerge simultaneously with knowledge, and integrating new knowledge into the model through fine-tuning is challenging, as it quickly corrupts its existing parametric memories. Our results emphasize the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggest novel data scheduling strategies to accelerate neural network training.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval and Consolidation in Large Language Models through Function Tokens
papers.research_question: How is memory retrieved during inference and consolidated during pre-training in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Function Token Hypothesis to explain memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs, where function tokens activate predictive features during inference and drive feature learning during pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes and provides evidence for the Function Token Hypothesis, which explains how function tokens drive memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
During inference, a small set of function tokens activate the majority of the model's features.
Function tokens dynamically reactivate the most predictive features from the context to guide next-token prediction.
During pre-training, the prediction of content tokens following function tokens dominates the loss and drives feature expansion.
Pre-training initially focuses on learning to predict function tokens before learning content tokens.
Scaling model size primarily enhances the prediction of content tokens.
papers.limitation: The paper does not explain how function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
future_direction: How function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
How post-training modifies activation patterns in function tokens.
The dynamics of feature formation and the underlying reason for the scale-free property of token-feature activation.
papers.abstract: The remarkable success of large language models (LLMs) stems from their ability to consolidate vast amounts of knowledge into the memory during pre-training and to retrieve it from the memory during inference, enabling advanced capabilities such as knowledge memorization, instruction-following and reasoning. However, the mechanisms of memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs remain poorly understood. In this paper, we propose the function token hypothesis to explain the workings of LLMs: During inference, function tokens activate the most predictive features from context and govern next token prediction (memory retrieval). During pre-training, predicting the next tokens (usually content tokens) that follow function tokens increases the number of learned features of LLMs and updates the model parameters (memory consolidation). Function tokens here roughly correspond to function words in linguistics, including punctuation marks, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions, in contrast to content tokens. We provide extensive experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis. Using bipartite graph analysis, we show that a small number of function tokens activate the majority of features. Case studies further reveal how function tokens activate the most predictive features from context to direct next token prediction. We also find that during pre-training, the training loss is dominated by predicting the next content tokens following function tokens, which forces the function tokens to select the most predictive features from context.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: AbsenceBench: Language Models Can't Tell What's Missing
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) identify information that has been deliberately omitted from documents?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AbsenceBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to detect omitted information, and shows that even state-of-the-art models perform poorly on this task despite excelling at related tasks like finding inserted information.
papers.conclusion: Current LLMs have a core limitation in detecting absent information, which is distinct from recalling present content. The results motivate future work on absence-aware architectures and evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform poorly on detecting omitted information even in medium-length contexts (average 5K tokens), with top models like Claude-3.7-Sonnet achieving only 69.6% F1-score.
Inference-time compute (e.g., chain-of-thought) offers only a modest performance improvement (7.9% on average) at the cost of generating an average of 8K extra thinking tokens.
Explicitly marking omissions with placeholder tokens (e.g., '<missing line>') improves model performance by 35.7% on average, suggesting a fundamental weakness in Transformer attention mechanisms for representing 'gaps'.
Models find it significantly harder to identify omissions than insertions, with an average 56.9% performance drop compared to the Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) test.
Longer context lengths and lower omission rates make the task harder for models, which is counter-intuitive as fewer omissions increase difficulty.
papers.limitation:
The benchmark only tests surface-form absence (exact text omission), not more subtle or semantic notions of absence like missing reasoning steps or evidence.
The structured task format (providing both original and modified documents side-by-side) may not reflect naturalistic settings where explicit comparisons are not provided.
The evaluation scope is limited to three domains (poetry, numerical sequences, GitHub PRs) and medium-length contexts (5K tokens on average), and may not generalize to other modalities, domains, or longer contexts.
No prompt tuning or in-context learning examples were explored due to cost constraints, leaving open whether more elaborate prompting could improve performance.
No statistical significance testing or error bars were computed due to API cost constraints.
future_direction: Examining more elaborate prompting strategies, including prompt tuning and in-context examples.
Extending the benchmark to other modalities (e.g., vision, audio), domains (e.g., legal, medical), and longer contexts.
Future architecture and inference-time research to make models more effective at handling and identifying absence.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable of processing long inputs and locating specific information within them, as evidenced by their performance on the Needle in a Haystack (NIAH) test. However, while models excel at recalling surprising information, they still struggle to identify clearly omitted information. We introduce AbsenceBench to assesses LLMs' capacity to detect missing information across three domains: numerical sequences, poetry, and GitHub pull requests. AbsenceBench asks models to identify which pieces of a document were deliberately removed, given access to both the original and edited contexts. Despite the apparent straightforwardness of these tasks, our experiments reveal that even state-of-the-art models like Claude-3.7-Sonnet achieve only 69.6% F1-score with a modest average context length of 5K tokens. Our analysis suggests this poor performance stems from a fundamental limitation: Transformer attention mechanisms cannot easily attend to "gaps" in documents since these absences don't correspond to any specific keys that can be attended to. Overall, our results and analysis provide a case study of the close proximity of tasks where models are already superhuman (NIAH) and tasks where models breakdown unexpectedly (AbsenceBench).

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do cognitive elements of reasoning manifest in LLMs, and how do they differ from human reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements for reasoning and conducts a large-scale empirical analysis of human and LLM reasoning traces, revealing that LLMs underutilize cognitive elements correlated with success and that test-time reasoning guidance can improve performance.
papers.conclusion: The taxonomy provides a shared vocabulary for diagnosing reasoning failures and enables principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms, while models possess latent capabilities that can be elicited with structural guidance.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs underutilize cognitive elements that are correlated with success, especially on ill-structured problems.
Humans use more abstraction and conceptual processing, while LLMs rely on surface-level enumeration.
Test-time reasoning guidance that scaffolds successful cognitive structures improves performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems.
The research community focuses on easily quantifiable cognitive elements (like sequential organization) and neglects meta-cognitive controls (like self-awareness).
Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously.
papers.limitation:
Human participants are educated adults; comparison with children might yield different insights.
Models are tested on a limited set of problem types.
future_direction: Using the taxonomy for training and evaluation of LLMs
Developing cognitive architectures based on the taxonomy
Extending the analysis to more problem types and models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve complex problems yet fail on simpler variants, suggesting they achieve correct outputs through mechanisms fundamentally different from human reasoning. To understand this gap, we synthesize cognitive science research into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements spanning reasoning invariants, meta-cognitive controls, representations for organizing reasoning & knowledge, and transformation operations. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework and conduct the first large-scale empirical analysis of 192K traces from 18 models across text, vision, and audio, complemented by 54 human think-aloud traces, which we make publicly available. We find that models under-utilize cognitive elements correlated with success, narrowing to rigid sequential processing on ill-structured problems where diverse representations and meta-cognitive monitoring are critical. Human traces show more abstraction and conceptual processing, while models default to surface-level enumeration. Meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers reveals the research community concentrates on easily quantifiable elements (sequential organization: 55%, decomposition: 60%) but neglecting meta-cognitive controls (self-awareness: 16%) that correlate with success. Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously. Leveraging these patterns, we develop test-time reasoning guidance that automatically scaffold successful structures, improving performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems. By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables systematic diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

papers.title: Exposing Attention Glitches with Flip-Flop Language Modeling
papers.research_question: Why do large language models sometimes output factual inaccuracies and exhibit erroneous reasoning? The paper investigates the phenomenon of attention glitches as a potential cause.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of attention glitches in Transformers, introduces flip-flop language modeling (FFLM) as a synthetic benchmark to isolate these errors, and finds that Transformers exhibit a long tail of sporadic reasoning errors even on this simple task.
papers.conclusion: Attention glitches are a fundamental failure mode of Transformer architectures when processing long-range dependencies, and may account for some closed-domain hallucinations in natural language models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers exhibit a long, irregular tail of reasoning errors (attention glitches) on flip-flop language modeling, while LSTMs extrapolate perfectly.
Natural language models (e.g., GPT-4, Pythia) can process flip-flop languages but not robustly, with error rates amplifying with sequence length.
Training on out-of-distribution data (rare sequences) significantly reduces errors, more so than scaling model size or training data.
Attention-sharpening regularizers reduce reasoning errors by an order of magnitude by promoting sparse attention patterns.
No mitigation tried (including regularization, architecture changes, and scaling) completely eliminated attention glitches.
papers.limitation:
None of the attempted mitigations (regularization, architecture changes, scaling) were successful in driving the number of errors to exactly zero.
Attention patterns may not be fully reliable for interpretability, as they can interact with other components in non-intuitive ways.
future_direction: A more thorough study of the training dynamics of flip-flop tasks with attention-sharpening regularization.
Understanding how to build robust Transformer models and training pipelines at larger scales.
Investigating the connection between attention glitches and closed-domain hallucinations in natural language models.
papers.abstract: Why do large language models sometimes output factual inaccuracies and exhibit erroneous reasoning? The brittleness of these models, particularly when executing long chains of reasoning, currently seems to be an inevitable price to pay for their advanced capabilities of coherently synthesizing knowledge, pragmatics, and abstract thought. Towards making sense of this fundamentally unsolved problem, this work identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of attention glitches, in which the Transformer architecture's inductive biases intermittently fail to capture robust reasoning. To isolate the issue, we introduce flip-flop language modeling (FFLM), a parametric family of synthetic benchmarks designed to probe the extrapolative behavior of neural language models. This simple generative task requires a model to copy binary symbols over long-range dependencies, ignoring the tokens in between. We find that Transformer FFLMs suffer from a long tail of sporadic reasoning errors, some of which we can eliminate using various regularization techniques. Our preliminary mechanistic analyses show why the remaining errors may be very difficult to diagnose and resolve. We hypothesize that attention glitches account for (some of) the closed-domain hallucinations in natural LLMs.

papers.title: Interpreting Key Mechanisms of Factual Recall in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models perform factual recall, specifically how do they extract arguments from context and apply implicit functions through MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a detailed mechanistic interpretation of factual recall in transformers, introducing a method to decompose MLP outputs and identifying a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a pipeline for factual recall in transformers, proposes a novel analytic method for MLPs, and identifies a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism that can be mitigated to improve factual recall confidence.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific attention heads extract topic tokens and pass them to subsequent MLPs.
MLPs act as activations that amplify or erase individual attention head outputs in the residual stream.
Deep MLPs apply implicit functions by adding a task-aware component that redirects the residual stream towards the correct answer.
A universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer suppresses correct predictions, which can be mitigated using the proposed interpretation.
These mechanisms are consistent across models (GPT-2, OPT, Llama-2), tasks (country-capital, product-developer), and few-shot settings.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not explore how the model constructs task semantics within its shallow layers.
The origins of the identified mechanisms (e.g., why MLPs redirect the residual stream) need further research.
The proposed analysis method for decomposing MLP outputs requires preliminary human reasoning and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Exploring how task semantics are constructed in shallow layers through collaborative circuit paths.
Investigating the origins of the mechanisms, such as why MLP outputs are structured as y-x.
Developing more automated interpretation techniques for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we delve into several mechanisms employed by Transformer-based language models (LLMs) for factual recall tasks. We outline a pipeline consisting of three major steps: (1) Given a prompt ``The capital of France is,'' task-specific attention heads extract the topic token, such as ``France,'' from the context and pass it to subsequent MLPs. (2) As attention heads' outputs are aggregated with equal weight and added to the residual stream, the subsequent MLP acts as an ``activation,'' which either erases or amplifies the information originating from individual heads. As a result, the topic token ``France'' stands out in the residual stream. (3) A deep MLP takes ``France'' and generates a component that redirects the residual stream towards the direction of the correct answer, i.e., ``Paris.'' This procedure is akin to applying an implicit function such as ``get\_capital($X$),'' and the argument $X$ is the topic token information passed by attention heads. To achieve the above quantitative and qualitative analysis for MLPs, we proposed a novel analytic method aimed at decomposing the outputs of the MLP into components understandable by humans. Additionally, we observed a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer of models, which suppresses correct predictions. We mitigate this suppression by leveraging our interpretation to improve factual recall confidence. The above interpretations are evaluated across diverse tasks spanning various domains of factual knowledge, using various language models from the GPT-2 families, 1.3B OPT, up to 7B Llama-2, and in both zero- and few-shot setups.

papers.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
papers.research_question: Does circuit analysis interpretability scale to large language models, specifically for the algorithmic task of multiple-choice question answering?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that existing circuit analysis techniques (logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, activation patching) scale to a 70B parameter model, allowing identification and partial understanding of the circuit for multiple-choice question answering, particularly 'correct letter' heads.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analysis techniques can scale to large models, but the features used to implement algorithmic tasks can be messy in their semantics, even when limited to a distribution with little superposition.
papers.key_findings:
Identified 45 nodes (attention heads and MLPs) that are causally responsible for most of the model's performance on the multiple-choice task.
Categorized attention heads into four types: 'Correct Letter', 'Uniform', 'Single Letter', and 'Amplification'.
Found that 'correct letter' heads attend to the correct answer label and copy it to the output logits.
Used SVD to compress query/key/value subspaces of 'correct letter' heads, finding the query and key subspaces represent an 'Nth item in an enumeration' feature, but this is only a partial explanation for behavior on a more general distribution.
Showed that the algorithmic task of mapping the correct answer to its label is interpretable, but the specific features used are messy and only partially understood.
papers.limitation:
The effect of patching a node can be compensated by downstream nodes (backup behavior), potentially distorting results.
The analysis only finds a cross-section of the circuit (nodes separating ancestors and descendants) rather than the full set of relevant nodes.
Results are only applicable to the specific distribution tested (MMLU subset).
Focused on the net effect on the correct label, neglecting the part of the circuit that identifies the set of possible answer tokens.
future_direction: Investigating the rest of the circuit (nodes feeding into the correct letter heads).
Comparing different approaches to causal interventions (e.g., noising vs. denoising).
Automating circuit analysis to reduce labor intensity.
papers.abstract: \emph{Circuit analysis} is a promising technique for understanding the internal mechanisms of language models. However, existing analyses are done in small models far from the state of the art. To address this, we present a case study of circuit analysis in the 70B Chinchilla model, aiming to test the scalability of circuit analysis. In particular, we study multiple-choice question answering, and investigate Chinchilla's capability to identify the correct answer \emph{label} given knowledge of the correct answer \emph{text}. We find that the existing techniques of logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, and activation patching naturally scale to Chinchilla, allowing us to identify and categorize a small set of `output nodes' (attention heads and MLPs). We further study the `correct letter' category of attention heads aiming to understand the semantics of their features, with mixed results. For normal multiple-choice question answers, we significantly compress the query, key and value subspaces of the head without loss of performance when operating on the answer labels for multiple-choice questions, and we show that the query and key subspaces represent an `Nth item in an enumeration' feature to at least some extent. However, when we attempt to use this explanation to understand the heads' behaviour on a more general distribution including randomized answer labels, we find that it is only a partial explanation, suggesting there is more to learn about the operation of `correct letter' heads on multiple choice question answering.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Cutting Off the Head Ends the Conflict: A Mechanism for Interpreting and Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism of knowledge conflicts in language models, and how can they be mitigated by precise interventions at the pivotal point?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that knowledge conflicts in language models arise from the integration of inconsistent information flows by memory heads and context heads in later layers, and proposes a parameter-free method (PH3) to mitigate conflicts by pruning these heads.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a mechanistic interpretation of knowledge conflicts in LMs and demonstrates that the proposed PH3 method can effectively mitigate these conflicts and control model behavior, showing strong generalization across models, relations, and data formats.
papers.key_findings:
FFNs in early layers enrich the semantic information of input elements, while MHAs in middle and late layers are crucial for passing information to the last token.
The last token extracts attribute information from the context subject (internal memory) and context attribute (external context) in later layers.
Some attention heads in late MHAs play opposite roles: memory heads recall knowledge from internal memory, and context heads retrieve knowledge from external context.
The pivotal point of knowledge conflict is the integration of inconsistent information flows by memory heads and context heads.
The proposed PH3 method can flexibly control LMs to use internal memory (↑44.0%) or external context (↑38.5%) by pruning conflicting attention heads without updating parameters.

papers.title: Editing Factual Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KNOWLEDGE EDITOR, a hyper-network-based method to edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning, while preserving other knowledge and ensuring consistency across paraphrases.
papers.conclusion: KNOWLEDGE EDITOR provides an effective and reliable method for editing factual knowledge in language models, meeting desiderata of generality, reliability, and consistency.
papers.key_findings:
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR achieves high success rate and retain accuracy on fact-checking and question answering tasks.
Using paraphrase supervision during training improves consistency across semantically equivalent inputs.
The updates predicted by KNOWLEDGE EDITOR are sparse and concentrated on attention weight matrices in lower layers, contrasting with gradient-based methods.
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR outperforms fine-tuning and constrained fine-tuning baselines in terms of retaining previous knowledge and generalization to paraphrases.
The hyper-network learns to project gradients to a different direction that preserves other knowledge while editing the target fact.
future_direction: Exploring multiple updates in a loop for editing.
Investigating the mechanism of knowledge encoding in LMs through the lens of editing.
papers.abstract: The factual knowledge acquired during pretraining and stored in the parameters of Language Models (LMs) can be useful in downstream tasks (e.g., question answering or textual inference). However, some facts can be incorrectly induced or become obsolete over time. We present KNOWLEDGEEDITOR, a method which can be used to edit this knowledge and, thus, fix 'bugs' or unexpected predictions without the need for expensive retraining or fine-tuning. Besides being computationally efficient, KNOWLEDGEEDITOR does not require any modifications in LM pretraining (e.g., the use of meta-learning). In our approach, we train a hyper-network with constrained optimization to modify a fact without affecting the rest of the knowledge; the trained hyper-network is then used to predict the weight update at test time. We show KNOWL-EDGEEDITOR's efficacy with two popular architectures and knowledge-intensive tasks: i) a BERT model fine-tuned for fact-checking, and ii) a sequence-to-sequence BART model for question answering. With our method, changing a prediction on the specific wording of a query tends to result in a consistent change in predictions also for its paraphrases. We show that this can be further encouraged by exploiting (e.g., automatically-generated) paraphrases during training. Interestingly, our hyper-network can be regarded as a 'probe' revealing which components need to be changed to manipulate factual knowledge; our analysis shows that the updates tend to be concentrated on a small subset of components. 1 How is Namibia's capital city called? papers.title: Understanding Verbatim Memorization in LLMs Through Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: What specific circuits in the model are responsible for initiating and maintaining verbatim memorization, and how do they differ from non-memorized generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using contrastive datasets and circuit discovery to identify circuits responsible for memorization in LLMs, finding that initiation circuits can also maintain memorization, but maintenance circuits cannot initiate it, and that memorization prevention transfers across domains while induction is context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that memorization initiation and maintenance are handled by different circuits, with initiation circuits being more general and maintenance circuits being more specific. Memorization prevention transfers across domains, while induction is context-dependent.
papers.key_findings:
Created two distinct contrastive datasets for memorization decision and branch comparison tasks.
Discovered compact circuits (≤5% of model edges) for memorization decision and branch comparison tasks using attribution patching techniques.
Circuits that initiate memorization can also maintain it once started, while circuits that only maintain memorization cannot trigger its initiation.
Memorization prevention mechanisms transfer robustly across different text domains (GitHub, Enron Emails, Common Crawl), while memorization induction appears more context-dependent.
Removing memorization (noising approach) is easier than inducing memorization (denoising approach) in the studied setup.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on Edge Attribution Patching with Integrated Gradients (EAP-IG) for circuit discovery, which provides only an approximation and may not fully correlate with direct activation patching measurements.
Findings are limited to a single, relatively small language model (GPT-Neo-125m); larger models might employ more complex or differently distributed memorization mechanisms.
Uncertainty about whether the identified circuits represent general memorization mechanisms or are specific to the Wikipedia subset of The Pile or artifacts of the contrastive dataset construction.
future_direction: Investigate how memorization mechanisms scale with model size.
Explore whether similar circuits exist in different model architectures.
Expand testing to more diverse datasets and memorization criteria to establish the generality of these mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Underlying mechanisms of memorization in LLMs-the verbatim reproduction of training data-remain poorly understood.What exact part of the network decides to retrieve a token that we would consider as start of memorization sequence?How exactly is the models' behaviour different when producing memorized sentence vs non-memorized?In this work we approach these questions from mechanistic interpretability standpoint by utilizing transformer circuits-the minimal computational subgraphs that perform specific functions within the model.Through carefully constructed contrastive datasets, we identify points where model generation diverges from memorized content and isolate the specific circuits responsible for two distinct aspects of memorization.We find that circuits that initiate memorization can also maintain it once started, while circuits that only maintain memorization cannot trigger its initiation.Intriguingly, memorization prevention mechanisms transfer robustly across different text domains, while memorization induction appears more contextdependent. 1

papers.title: How Do Large Language Models Acquire Factual Knowledge During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge acquired during LLM pretraining, and how are LLMs affected by the training data at each step? How do training conditions affect the effectivity of factual knowledge acquisition? How is acquired factual knowledge forgotten, and how does training conditions affect forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during LLM pretraining, revealing that acquisition occurs by accumulating small probability increases with each encounter, but is diluted by subsequent forgetting. It also finds that effectivity does not improve with more pretraining data, but model size helps, and forgetting follows a power-law.
papers.conclusion: Factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining is a process of incremental probability increases countered by forgetting, and this understanding can explain phenomena like poor long-tail knowledge performance and the benefits of deduplication.
papers.key_findings:
Factual knowledge acquisition occurs by accumulating micro-acquisitions (small increases in log probability) with subsequent forgetting each time the model encounters the knowledge during pretraining.
Effectivity (immediate improvement in log probability) does not improve with more pretraining tokens, but does improve with larger model size.
Forgetting of acquired factual knowledge follows a power-law relationship with training steps (or tokens).
Training with duplicated data leads to faster forgetting compared to paraphrased data, highlighting the importance of deduplication.
Training with larger batch sizes makes models more robust to forgetting, enhancing knowledge acquisition.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent observation that large language models (LLMs) can store substantial factual knowledge, there is a limited understanding of the mechanisms of how they acquire factual knowledge through pretraining. This work addresses this gap by studying how LLMs acquire factual knowledge during pretraining. The findings reveal several important insights into the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during pretraining. First, counterintuitively, we observe that pretraining on more data shows no significant improvement in the model's capability to acquire and maintain factual knowledge. Next, there is a power-law relationship between training steps and forgetting of memorization and generalization of factual knowledge, and LLMs trained with duplicated training data exhibit faster forgetting. Third, training LLMs with larger batch sizes can enhance the models' robustness to forgetting. Overall, our observations suggest that factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining occurs by progressively increasing the probability of factual knowledge presented in the pretraining data at each step. However, this increase is diluted by subsequent forgetting. Based on this interpretation, we demonstrate that we can provide plausible explanations for recently observed behaviors of LLMs, such as the poor performance of LLMs on long-tail knowledge and the benefits of deduplicating the pretraining corpus.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Language Models Remember Facts?
papers.research_question: How do factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs, and when does language play a role in recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs with variations, and reveals that the last token acts as a function vector encoding relation and language, composed in two stages in decoder-only models.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for factual recall, indicating that knowledge evaluation and editing methods need to be adapted for multilingual settings.
papers.key_findings:
The early MLP site for subject enrichment is present in multilingual LLMs, but the late site involves both MLP and attention, unlike English LLMs where only attention dominates.
Subject information flows similarly to monolingual models, but non-subject token flow differs.
In multilingual decoder-only LLMs, both feed-forward and attention sublayers contribute to object extraction, unlike in English autoregressive LLMs where attention modules dominate.
The last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV) encoding both the relation and the output language.
In decoder-only LLMs, the FV is constructed in two distinct phases: first encoding the relation, then incorporating the language.
future_direction: Developing knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition methods tailored for multilingual LLMs
Studying how the function vector is altered across languages to understand if models think in English
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) store and retrieve vast amounts of factual knowledge acquired during pre-training. Prior research has localized and identified mechanisms behind knowledge recall; however, it has only focused on English monolingual models. The question of how these mechanisms generalize to non-English languages and multilingual LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of three multilingual LLMs. First, we show that previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture. Next, through patching intermediate representations, we localize the role of language during recall, finding that subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent. Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of knowledge neurons and a gradient-based attribution method to identify them in pretrained Transformers, demonstrating their role in storing factual knowledge and enabling model editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons (knowledge neurons) within feed-forward networks, and these neurons can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed attribution method are positively correlated with the expression of specific factual knowledge.
Suppressing or amplifying the activation of identified knowledge neurons significantly decreases or increases the probability of the correct answer, respectively.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts expressing their corresponding fact than by control prompts.
Knowledge neurons can be used to update or erase specific factual knowledge in the model with minimal impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Examines knowledge neurons based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain underexplored.
Focuses on factual knowledge for ease of evaluation, though the method is applicable to other knowledge types.
Uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Explore interactions between knowledge neurons.
Extend the method to other types of knowledge beyond factual knowledge.
Extend to multi-word blanks in cloze queries.
Investigate knowledge neurons in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus. In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: Time Course MechInterp: Analyzing the Evolution of Components and Knowledge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Which components (attention heads, FFNs) contribute to solving factual knowledge tasks, and how do these circuits for factual knowledge evolve over the course of model training?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides a mechanistic view of how factual knowledge representation evolves during LLM pre-training, showing that models initially rely on general-purpose components which later specialize, with attention heads exhibiting high turnover and FFNs remaining more stable.
papers.conclusion: The study offers insights into the hierarchical learning process of LLMs, where general components form first and later diversify, with attention heads being highly adaptive and FFNs providing stable processing.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads show high turnover and dynamic role transitions, while FFNs are more stable throughout training.
Location-based relations (LOC) converge to high accuracy earlier in training than name-based relations (NAME).
LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.
Answer-specific attention heads demonstrate the highest turnover, indicating frequent role changes.
FFNs act as a steady processing backbone, with most remaining in general roles.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints prevented analysis at the neuron level and the use of alternative interpretability techniques like activation patching across all snapshots.
The dataset is limited to English and covers only location-based and name-based factual relations.
The analysis uses a fixed activation threshold for role classification, which may introduce bias.
Only a subset of training snapshots was analyzed, leaving gaps in tracking role transitions.
Direct comparison with other model families (e.g., Pythia) was not feasible due to architectural differences preventing the use of IFRs.
future_direction: Incorporate more diverse datasets, additional model variants, and alternative interpretability techniques.
Expand analysis to other domains, multilingual settings, and ambiguous queries.
Investigate the long-term impact of component dynamics on fine-tuning, pruning, and continual learning.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) acquire and store factual knowledge is crucial for enhancing their interpretability and reliability.In this work, we analyze the evolution of factual knowledge representation in the OLMo-7B model by tracking the roles of its attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) over the course of pre-training.We classify these components into four roles: general, entity, relation-answer, and fact-answer specific and examine their stability and transitions.Our results show that LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.Once the model reliably predicts answers, some components are repurposed, suggesting an adaptive learning process.Notably, attention heads display the highest turnover.We also present evidence that FFNs remain more stable throughout training.Furthermore, our probing experiments reveal that location-based relations converge to high accuracy earlier in training than namebased relations, highlighting how task complexity shapes acquisition dynamics.These insights offer a mechanistic view of knowledge formation in LLMs.We release the code and data. 1

papers.title: Too Late to Recall: Explaining the Two-Hop Problem in Multimodal Knowledge Retrieval
papers.research_question: Why do many vision language models (VLMs) exhibit reduced factual recall performance compared to their large language model (LLM) backbones, and what is the underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs suffer from a 'two-hop problem' where entity representations from visual inputs emerge too late in the forward pass, bypassing the early-layer MLP circuits in the LLM backbone responsible for factual recall, leading to performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: The speed of early entity resolution critically determines how effective VLMs are in using preexisting LLM mechanisms; representation misalignment limits VLMs' ability to reuse existing task circuits.
papers.key_findings:
11 out of 14 benchmarked VLMs exhibit factual recall degradation compared to their LLM backbones.
Attribution patching shows degraded VLMs do not use the same early-layer MLPs as their LLM backbones for factual recall.
Activation patching of early-layer MLP outputs from the LLM into the VLM recovers performance, indicating these components are causally crucial.
Linear probing reveals entity representations emerge in middle-to-late layers in degraded VLMs, but early in high-performing VLMs.
Chain-of-thought prompting can mitigate the performance gap for some VLMs, especially larger ones.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on factual recall and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Investigate better, more data-efficient adapter mechanisms and multimodal alignment techniques.
Examine other tasks beyond factual recall, comparing VLMs against their LLM backbone.
papers.abstract: Training vision language models (VLMs) aims to align visual representations from a vision encoder with the textual representations of a pretrained large language model (LLM). However, many VLMs exhibit reduced factual recall performance compared to their LLM backbones, raising the question of how effective multimodal fine-tuning is at extending existing mechanisms within the LLM to visual inputs. We argue that factual recall based on visual inputs requires VLMs to solve a two-hop problem: (1) forming entity representations from visual inputs, and (2) recalling associated factual knowledge based on these entity representations. By benchmarking 14 VLMs with various architectures (LLaVA, Native, Cross-Attention), sizes (7B-124B parameters), and training setups on factual recall tasks against their original LLM backbone models, we find that 11 of 14 models exhibit factual recall degradation. We select three models with high and two models with low performance degradation, and use attribution patching, activation patching, and probing to show that degraded VLMs struggle to use the existing factual recall circuit of their LLM backbone, because they resolve the first hop too late in the computation. In contrast, high-performing VLMs resolve entity representations early enough to reuse the existing factual recall mechanism. Finally, we demonstrate two methods to recover performance: patching entity representations from the LLM backbone into the VLM, and prompting with chain-of-thought reasoning. Our results highlight that the speed of early entity resolution critically determines how effective VLMs are in using preexisting LLM mechanisms. More broadly, our work illustrates how mechanistic analysis can explain and unveil systematic failures in multimodal alignment.

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized.
