We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: Memorization Without Overfitting: Analyzing the Training Dynamics of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do memorization and forgetting dynamics in language models change during training, and how do they depend on factors like model size, dataset size, and learning rate?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models memorize training data faster and forget less throughout training, with nouns and numbers being memorized more quickly than other parts of speech.
papers.conclusion: Memorization dynamics are a critical metric for understanding language model training, with larger models exhibiting faster memorization and less forgetting, highlighting the importance of analyzing memorization alongside cross-entropy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Larger language models memorize training data faster across various settings (causal and masked LM, different dataset sizes).
Larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before overfitting occurs.
Forgetting curves approach a baseline (the forgetting baseline), and this baseline increases with model scale, meaning larger models forget less.
Nouns and numbers are memorized much faster than other parts of speech, acting as unique identifiers for training examples.
Adding unique identifiers (like document IDs) to training examples increases memorization speed.
papers.limitation:
The exact memorization metric (Definition 1) ignores model confidence and does not normalize for duplication in the training set.
The focus on exact memorization may not capture all aspects of privacy, as it only considers verbatim output of sensitive information.
future_direction: Understanding the structure of the forgetting baseline, e.g., what types of tokens (parts of speech, synonyms, facts) are memorized in the baseline.
Analyzing memorization dynamics as a critical metric when scaling up language models, beyond just cross-entropy loss.
papers.abstract: Despite their wide adoption, the underlying training and memorization dynamics of very large language models is not well understood. We empirically study exact memorization in causal and masked language modeling, across model sizes and throughout the training process. We measure the effects of dataset size, learning rate, and model size on memorization, finding that larger language models memorize training data faster across all settings. Surprisingly, we show that larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before over-fitting and tend to forget less throughout the training process. We also analyze the memorization dynamics of different parts of speech and find that models memorize nouns and numbers first; we hypothesize and provide empirical evidence that nouns and numbers act as a unique identifier for memorizing individual training examples. Together, these findings present another piece of the broader puzzle of trying to understand what actually improves as models get bigger.

papers.title: Knowing When to Stop: Efficient Context Processing via Latent Sufficiency Signals
papers.research_question: Can we enable LLMs to self-assess context sufficiency and terminate early without compromising accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces dynamic context cutoff, a method that uses internal sufficiency signals in attention heads to enable LLMs to stop processing context early, achieving token reduction and accuracy improvement.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic context cutoff enables LLMs to process only minimal necessary context by detecting sufficiency signals internally, reducing tokens by 1.33× and improving accuracy by 3.4%, outperforming static methods.
papers.key_findings:
Specific attention heads encode latent sufficiency signals detectable via lightweight classifiers.
The method achieves an average token reduction of 1.33× and accuracy improvement of 3.4%.
Larger models (14B+) exhibit emergent self-assessment capabilities through prompting.
The method outperforms static context compression methods like RAG and LLMLingua.
Sufficiency detection is more reliable through internal activations than surface-level outputs.
papers.limitation:
Applicability to all task types (e.g., creative writing, open-ended dialogue) remains an open question.
Relies on validation-based hyperparameter tuning for threshold selection.
future_direction: Investigate classifier performance across broader task spectrums.
Develop adaptive threshold selection mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process entire input contexts indiscriminately, which is inefficient when the information required to answer a query is localized within the context. We present dynamic context cutoff, a novel method enabling LLMs to self-terminate processing upon acquiring sufficient task-relevant information. Through analysis of model internals, we discover that specific attention heads inherently encode "sufficiency signals" -- detectable through lightweight classifiers -- that predict when critical information has been processed. This reveals a new efficiency paradigm: models' internal understanding naturally dictates processing needs rather than external compression heuristics. Comprehensive experiments across six QA datasets (up to 40K tokens) with three model families (LLaMA/Qwen/Mistral, 1B-70B) demonstrate 3.4% accuracy improvement while achieving 1.33x token reduction on average. Furthermore, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to other context efficiency methods at equivalent token reduction rates. Additionally, we observe an emergent scaling phenomenon: while smaller models require probing for sufficiency detection, larger models exhibit intrinsic self-assessment capabilities through prompting.

papers.title: Where Knowledge Collides: A Mechanistic Study of Intra-Memory Knowledge Conflict in Language Models
papers.research_question: Which internal components of language models are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training data, and can noisy or incorrect information be selectively suppressed during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a mechanistic interpretability framework to localize and intervene on conflicting knowledge encoded in language models, showing that attention components in later layers play a key role in encoding and resolving such conflicts.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a mechanistic interpretability framework to study intra-memory knowledge conflict, demonstrating that logit inspection, activation patching, and cross-model patching can localize and intervene on conflicting internal representations at inference time.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting training data reduces model confidence and introduces confusion in later layers.
Attention components in later layers dominate in shaping factual responses and encoding conflicting knowledge.
Activation patching can steer model generation toward accurate outputs, with success rates varying across models (up to 22% for GPT-2 XL and 70% for Qwen3-4B).
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) improves steering success and reduces noise compared to standard activation patching, especially for certain conflict attributes.
Findings generalize across different model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B), though intervention effectiveness varies.
papers.limitation:
Limited set of conflict types and restriction to a 1:1 ratio of conflicting information per entity.
Results are presented on a limited set of model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B).
The underlying factors that drive the model's preference for one conflicting fact over another are not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend these methods to knowledge editing and robust information tracing across prompts and model variants.
Include more conflict types and multiple conflicting information per entity.
Evaluate across additional model families.
papers.abstract: In language models (LMs), intra-memory knowledge conflict largely arises when inconsistent information about the same event is encoded within the model's parametric knowledge. While prior work has primarily focused on resolving conflicts between a model's internal knowledge and external resources through approaches such as fine-tuning or knowledge editing, the problem of localizing conflicts that originate during pre-training within the model's internal representations remain unexplored. In this work, we design a framework based on mechanistic interpretability methods to identify where and how conflicting knowledge from the pre-training data is encoded within LMs. Our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence that specific internal components of a language model are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training, and we demonstrate how mechanistic interpretability methods can be leveraged to causally intervene in and control conflicting knowledge at inference time.

papers.title: Your Context Is Not an Array: Unveiling Random Access Limitations in Transformers
papers.research_question: Why do Transformer-based large language models fail at length generalization in algorithmic tasks? The paper hypothesizes that this failure is due to their inability to perform random memory accesses (index-based addressing) within the context window.
papers.core_contribution: Transformers struggle with length generalization in algorithmic tasks because they cannot perform random memory access (index-based addressing); this can be mitigated by using content-based addressing via mnemonics or by restructuring the scratchpad to avoid random access.
papers.conclusion: Transformers' attention mechanism is well-suited for content-based addressing but struggles with random token access, which is crucial for algorithmic reasoning. Equipping Transformers with index-based addressing mechanisms could enable them to learn algorithmic tasks more generally.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers fail at length generalization in algorithmic tasks like parity and addition due to their inability to perform random memory access (index-based addressing).
Using an interleaved scratchpad format that places the current active bit and running parity adjacent eliminates the need for random access and enables perfect length generalization.
Adding mnemonics (random tokens) to the scratchpad allows Transformers to perform random access indirectly via content-based addressing, enabling length generalization.
Attention map visualizations show that without mnemonics, the model fails to attend to the correct bit beyond the training length, while with mnemonics, the attention pattern is near-perfect.
The effectiveness of mnemonics depends on their alignment between input and output and their randomness; constant or non-aligned mnemonics do not work.
future_direction: Equipping Transformers with effective index-based addressing mechanisms to enable learning of algorithmic tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite their recent successes, Transformer-based large language models show surprising failure modes. A well-known example of such failure modes is their inability to length-generalize: solving problem instances at inference time that are longer than those seen during training. In this work, we further explore the root cause of this failure by performing a detailed analysis of model behaviors on the simple parity task. Our analysis suggests that length generalization failures are intricately related to a model's inability to perform random memory accesses within its context window. We present supporting evidence for this hypothesis by demonstrating the effectiveness of methodologies that circumvent the need for indexing or that enable random token access indirectly, through content-based addressing. We further show where and how the failure to perform random memory access manifests through attention map visualizations.

papers.title: Is Bigger and Deeper Always Better? Probing LLaMA Across Scales and Layers
papers.research_question: Does increasing model size and depth improve LLaMA's intrinsic understanding and advanced capabilities like reasoning and calculation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that increasing model size does not automatically impart additional knowledge or computational prowess but can enhance reasoning abilities and reduce hallucinations beyond certain thresholds. Also, lower layers lack arithmetic and factual knowledge but possess logical thinking and multilingual abilities, while top layers house computational power and real-world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Beyond generation, the study uses probing tasks to reveal that LLaMA models have nearly identical computational abilities and factual knowledge regardless of scale, while increasing size benefits reasoning. Lower layers contain multilingual features and reasoning abilities but lack computational skills and real-world knowledge, which are housed in the top layers.
papers.key_findings:
Horizontally, enlarging model sizes almost could not automatically impart additional knowledge or computational prowess. Instead, it can enhance reasoning abilities, especially in math problem solving, and helps reduce hallucinations, but only beyond certain size thresholds.
Vertically, the lower layers of LLaMA lack substantial arithmetic and factual knowledge, showcasing logical thinking, multilingual and recognitive abilities, with top layers housing most computational power and real-world knowledge.
The optimal performance in math problem solving and computational abilities is not always at the final layer, but often in several layers before the last. For factual knowledge, the final layer is crucial.
In cross-lingual reasoning, performance decreases as layers deepen, indicating that earlier layers preserve multilingual features.
Lower layers across different model scales show similar abilities.
papers.limitation:
Why LLaMA obtains optimal performances in their last 2-7 layers rather than the absolute final layer in some tasks like computation?
Why the penultimate layer of LLaMA performs much better than the last layer in cross-lingual math problem solving tasks?
Why essentially all LLaMA models begin to show significant performance improvements starting from their mid-layer networks?
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth analysis of Large Language Models (LLMs), focusing on LLaMA, a prominent open-source foundational model in natural language processing. Instead of assessing LLaMA through its generative output, we design multiple-choice tasks to probe its intrinsic understanding in high-order tasks such as reasoning and computation. We examine the model horizontally, comparing different sizes, and vertically, assessing different layers. We unveil several key and uncommon findings based on the designed probing tasks: (1) Horizontally, enlarging model sizes almost could not automatically impart additional knowledge or computational prowess. Instead, it can enhance reasoning abilities, especially in math problem solving, and helps reduce hallucinations, but only beyond certain size thresholds; (2) In vertical analysis, the lower layers of LLaMA lack substantial arithmetic and factual knowledge, showcasing logical thinking, multilingual and recognitive abilities, with top layers housing most computational power and real-world knowledge.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Differentiation of Memorization and Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do distinct sets of neurons underlie memorization and generalization behaviors in LLMs? Can targeted neuron-level interventions at inference time steer model behavior toward memorization or generalization? Are the observed neuron-behavior associations consistent across retraining runs and transferable across different tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that memorization and generalization activate distinct neuron subsets within LLMs, and that intervening on these subsets can controllably alter model behavior, with these neuron-behavior mappings being stable across intra-task and inter-task variations.
papers.conclusion: Memorization and generalization are encoded in separable neural pathways within LLMs, enabling inference-time steering and revealing consistent functional modularity.
papers.key_findings:
Distinct neuron subsets are responsible for memorization and generalization behaviors in LLMs.
Inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward memorization or generalization.
The neuron-behavior associations are consistent across retraining runs on the same task (intra-task consistency).
Neurons identified from one task can transfer to another task to some extent (inter-task transferability).
Behavior-associated signals originate primarily in the pretrained base model rather than the LoRA adapter.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to GPT-2 and LLaMA 3.2 models, lacking validation on diverse architectures and scales.
Evaluation uses only two task types (induction-style in-context inference and arithmetic addition), not capturing the breadth of language tasks.
The operationalization of generalization is comparatively less complete than memorization, capturing only specific forms.
The inference-time intervention uses a straightforward linear neuron-shifting method, which may not be optimal.
future_direction: Broader validation on diverse architectures and scales.
Examination of more varied tasks such as QA, commonsense reasoning, or dialogue.
Development of improved neuron selection methods for higher behavioral specificity.
papers.abstract: We investigate how Large Language Models (LLMs) distinguish between memorization and generalization at the neuron level. Through carefully designed tasks, we identify distinct neuron subsets responsible for each behavior. Experiments on both a GPT-2 model trained from scratch and a pretrained LLaMA-3.2 model fine-tuned with LoRA show consistent neuron-level specialization. We further demonstrate that inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward memorization or generalization. To assess robustness, we evaluate intra-task and inter-task consistency, confirming that these neuron-behavior associations reflect generalizable patterns rather than dataset-specific artifacts. Our findings reveal modular structure in LLMs and enable controlling memorization and generalization behaviors at inference time.

papers.title: Language Models Do Not Have Human-Like Working Memory
papers.research_question: Can large language models maintain and manipulate unexpressed internal representations (latent state persistence) analogous to human working memory?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs lack the ability to maintain persistent latent states (working memory), functioning instead as reactive post-hoc reasoners, which highlights a fundamental architectural divergence from human-like cognition.
papers.conclusion: Current LLMs lack the ability to persistently maintain and manipulate latent states, functioning as reactive post-hoc reasoners rather than proactive planners, which poses a bottleneck for autonomous agents and tasks requiring working memory.
papers.key_findings:
In the Number Guessing Game, LLMs fail to allocate probability mass to a singular hidden choice, violating the sum-of-probability identity.
In the Yes-No Game, as the number of questions increases, LLMs suffer from concept drift and inevitable self-contradictions due to lack of latent state persistence.
In Mathematical Mentalism, LLMs fail to track transformations on hidden variables, revealing a failure in variable binding and state evolution when the initial state is not explicitly present.
Scaling and long-reasoning traces (e.g., in o3-Mini or DeepSeek-R1) do not bridge the latent state persistence gap; the underlying latent persistence remains absent.
LLMs exhibit human-centric priors such as the 'Blue-Seven' phenomenon, indicating reliance on stochastic priors rather than committed internal states.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning abilities, we demonstrate that they lack a fundamental aspect of human cognition: working memory. Human working memory is an active cognitive system that enables not only the temporary storage of information but also its processing and utilization, enabling coherent reasoning and decision-making. Without working memory, individuals may produce unrealistic responses, exhibit self-contradictions, and struggle with tasks that require mental reasoning. Existing evaluations using N-back or context-dependent tasks fall short as they allow LLMs to exploit external context rather than retaining the reasoning process in the latent space. We introduce three novel tasks: (1) Number Guessing, (2) Yes-No Deduction, and (3) Math Magic, designed to isolate internal representation from external context. Across seventeen frontier models spanning four major model families, we consistently observe irrational or contradictory behaviors, indicating LLMs' inability to retain and manipulate latent information. Our work establishes a new benchmark for evaluating working memory in LLMs and highlights this limitation as a key bottleneck for advancing reliable reasoning systems. Code and prompts for the experiments are available at https://github.com/penguinnnnn/LLM-Working-Memory.

papers.title: When Can Transformers Count to n?
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental limitations of transformers on basic counting tasks, and how does the difficulty scale with embedding dimension, context length, and vocabulary size?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a sharp theoretical phase transition in transformers' ability to count, governed by the relationship between embedding dimension and vocabulary size. When the vocabulary exceeds the embedding dimension, counting becomes numerically unstable and practically unlearnable.
papers.conclusion: Transformers have a fundamental geometric bottleneck for counting tasks when vocabulary size exceeds embedding dimension, suggesting that relying on standard parallel attention is insufficient and external tools or sequential memory systems may be necessary.
papers.key_findings:
When the embedding dimension is at least as large as the vocabulary size, transformers can perfectly maintain token counts using orthogonal embeddings.
When the vocabulary size exceeds the embedding dimension, interference between non-orthogonal token representations forces network weights to scale polynomially, rendering exact counting numerically unstable and unlearnable.
Empirical training of small transformers shows a strict performance drop at the theoretical d=m threshold and catastrophic out-of-distribution failure when scaling vocabulary or context length.
State-of-the-art pretrained language models (Gemini, Gemma, Llama, Qwen, Phi) suffer from similar vulnerabilities, with performance degrading as vocabulary size or sequence length increases.
The vocabulary size, not just context length, fundamentally dictates the difficulty of aggregation tasks like counting in transformers.
papers.limitation: The theoretical framework's reliance on bounded Lipschitz constants to evaluate deep transformers; extending communication complexity lower bounds to deeper models without strict Lipschitz assumptions remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Exploring how the fundamental bottleneck behaves in massive-scale frontier models (100B+ parameters).
Rethinking standard discrete tokenization to improve algorithmic generalization, e.g., via continuous or random embeddings.
Using mechanistic interpretability to analyze the exact suboptimal heuristics transformers converge to during the d < m regime.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on the transformer architectures can solve highly complex tasks. But are there simple tasks that such models cannot solve? Here we focus on very simple counting tasks, that involve counting how many times a token in the vocabulary have appeared in a string. We show that if the dimension of the transformer state is linear in the context length, this task can be solved. However, the solution we propose does not scale beyond this limit, and we provide theoretical arguments for why it is likely impossible for a size limited transformer to implement this task. Our empirical results demonstrate the same phase-transition in performance, as anticipated by the theoretical argument. Our results demonstrate the importance of understanding how transformers can solve simple tasks.

papers.title: Does Time Have Its Place? Temporal Heads: Where Language Models Recall Time-specific Information
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how language models encode and recall time-specific information, focusing on whether there are specific attention heads dedicated to temporal knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers Temporal Heads, specific attention heads in language models that encode and recall time-specific knowledge, and shows that ablating them impairs temporal knowledge while leaving other capabilities intact.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Temporal Heads are crucial for temporal knowledge in LLMs, and targeting them can enable precise temporal updates without global retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Temporal Heads, such as a15.h0 and a18.h3 in Llama2, are identified across multiple models and are crucial for temporal knowledge recall.
Ablating Temporal Heads significantly reduces accuracy on temporal knowledge tasks but has minimal effect on time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance.
Temporal Heads are activated for both numerical (e.g., 'In 2004') and textual (e.g., 'In the year...') temporal conditions, indicating they encode a broad temporal dimension.
Temporal knowledge can be edited by adjusting the activations of these heads, enabling targeted updates.
Backup Temporal Heads exist that can compensate when primary heads are ablated, ensuring model robustness.
papers.limitation:
Analysis of unstructured temporal QAs was constrained due to lack of temporal dependencies in options.
EAP-IG does not support models with Grouped-Query Attention, limiting analysis of models like Llama-3.
future_direction: Future work should focus on broader application for enhancing temporal reasoning and time-aware model alignment.
papers.abstract: While the ability of language models to elicit facts has been widely investigated, how they handle temporally changing facts remains underexplored. We discover Temporal Heads, specific attention heads that primarily handle temporal knowledge, through circuit analysis. We confirm that these heads are present across multiple models, though their specific locations may vary, and their responses differ depending on the type of knowledge and its corresponding years. Disabling these heads degrades the model's ability to recall time-specific knowledge while maintaining its general capabilities without compromising time-invariant and question-answering performances. Moreover, the heads are activated not only numeric conditions ("In 2004") but also textual aliases ("In the year ..."), indicating that they encode a temporal dimension beyond simple numerical representation. Furthermore, we expand the potential of our findings by demonstrating how temporal knowledge can be edited by adjusting the values of these heads.

papers.title: Delving into the Reversal Curse: How Far Can Large Language Models Generalize?
papers.research_question: How does the reversal curse manifest across various tasks, and what are the underlying generalization abilities and problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that the reversal curse is more likely a backward recall deficiency, and identifies an inherent 'thinking bias' in LLMs where they preferentially use names to initiate fact recall, which strongly influences their generalization ability based on training data structure.
papers.conclusion: The reversal curse is a backward recall deficiency in decoder-only models, and LLMs' inherent thinking bias underscores the critical importance of appropriate training data structure for successful knowledge application and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can generalize to 'B is A' when both A and B are presented in context (e.g., in multiple-choice questions).
Generalization ability is highly correlated with the structure of training documents (works for '[Name] is [Description]' but not the reverse).
LLMs possess an inherent thinking bias: they consistently start fact recall with names provided in the query.
The negative impact of this bias on downstream task performance is hard to mitigate through training alone.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) showcase unprecedented capabilities, they also exhibit certain inherent limitations when facing seemingly trivial tasks. A prime example is the recently debated "reversal curse", which surfaces when models, having been trained on the fact "A is B", struggle to generalize this knowledge to infer that "B is A". In this paper, we examine the manifestation of the reversal curse across various tasks and delve into both the generalization abilities and the problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs. This investigation leads to a series of significant insights: (1) LLMs are able to generalize to "B is A" when both A and B are presented in the context as in the case of a multiple-choice question. (2) This generalization ability is highly correlated to the structure of the fact "A is B" in the training documents. For example, this generalization only applies to biographies structured in "[Name] is [Description]" but not to "[Description] is [Name]". (3) We propose and verify the hypothesis that LLMs possess an inherent bias in fact recalling during knowledge application, which explains and underscores the importance of the document structure to successful learning. (4) The negative impact of this bias on the downstream performance of LLMs can hardly be mitigated through training alone. These findings offer a novel perspective on interpreting LLMs' generalization through their intrinsic mechanisms and provide insights for developing more effective learning methods. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/alibaba/thinking_bias.git.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Disentangling Memory and Reasoning Ability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle memory recall and reasoning steps in large language models to improve performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel LLM inference paradigm that disentangles memory recall and reasoning steps using special tokens, enhancing both accuracy and interpretability in complex QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed decomposition of memory and reasoning steps in LLMs leads to improved performance and greater interpretability, enabling better error analysis and model refinement.
papers.key_findings:
The method improves LLM performance on StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, and TruthfulQA benchmarks, outperforming baselines like CoT and planning tokens.
On TruthfulQA, the enhanced LLaMA-3.1-8B model achieves 86.6% accuracy, surpassing GPT-4o with CoT prompting.
Error analysis reveals that most errors originate from reasoning steps rather than memory recall, highlighting reasoning as the primary challenge.
The decomposition enhances interpretability by allowing clear separation of memory and reasoning steps in the inference process.
Attention analysis shows that special tokens receive higher attention weights, indicating their role in guiding knowledge and reasoning content generation.
papers.limitation:
Dependency on training data quality for memory recall
Token utilization complexity due to special tokens
Performance may struggle with highly complex reasoning tasks
Computation overhead from decomposing steps
future_direction: Dynamic memory updating to incorporate new information without retraining.
Adaptive reasoning steps based on task complexity.
Interpretable error analysis tools for tracing failures to memory or reasoning steps.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in handling complex tasks requiring both extensive knowledge and reasoning abilities. However, the existing LLM inference pipeline operates as an opaque process without explicit separation between knowledge retrieval and reasoning steps, making the model's decision-making process unclear and disorganized. This ambiguity can lead to issues such as hallucinations and knowledge forgetting, which significantly impact the reliability of LLMs in high-stakes domains. In this paper, we propose a new inference paradigm that decomposes the complex inference process into two distinct and clear actions: (1) memory recall: which retrieves relevant knowledge, and (2) reasoning: which performs logical steps based on the recalled knowledge. To facilitate this decomposition, we introduce two special tokens memory and reason, guiding the model to distinguish between steps that require knowledge retrieval and those that involve reasoning. Our experiment results show that this decomposition not only improves model performance but also enhances the interpretability of the inference process, enabling users to identify sources of error and refine model responses effectively. The code is available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Disentangling-Memory-and-Reasoning.

papers.title: Algorithmic Phase Transitions in Language Models: A Mechanistic Case Study of Arithmetic
papers.research_question: How do language models achieve zero-shot performance on some tasks but not others? Specifically, do they use stable algorithms across related subtasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concepts of algorithmic stability and algorithmic phase transitions, and shows that language models exhibit sharp algorithmic phase transitions even on simple arithmetic tasks, which may explain poor generalization.
papers.conclusion: Language models are algorithmically unstable for two-operand addition, and this instability may be a barrier for generalization in logical reasoning. The introduced interpretability technique can help evaluate model design choices and serve as a diagnostic tool.
papers.key_findings:
Gemma-2-2b uses different computational subcircuits for addition problems with different digit lengths, indicating algorithmic instability.
The model undergoes sharp algorithmic phase transitions between symmetric, boundary, and interior addition tasks.
The structure of the identified subcircuits varies: symmetric tasks show top-heavy circuits, boundary tasks show two peaks of activation, and interior tasks show diffuse circuits.
Algorithmic instability correlates with lack of generalization in arithmetic performance.
The paper introduces methods to quantify algorithmic changes using activation patching and clustering techniques.
papers.limitation:
Relies on activation patching, which has known limitations.
Operationalizes algorithmic changes as structural changes, which may not capture all aspects of algorithmic change.
future_direction: Test the robustness of identified subcircuits by perturbing the weights of the network.
Explore other methods to quantify algorithmic changes beyond structural similarity.
papers.abstract: Zero-shot capabilities of large language models make them powerful tools for solving a range of tasks without explicit training. It remains unclear, however, how these models achieve such performance, or why they can zero-shot some tasks but not others. In this paper, we shed some light on this phenomenon by defining and investigating algorithmic stability in language models -- changes in problem-solving strategy employed by the model as a result of changes in task specification. We focus on a task where algorithmic stability is needed for generalization: two-operand arithmetic. Surprisingly, we find that Gemma-2-2b employs substantially different computational models on closely related subtasks, i.e. four-digit versus eight-digit addition. Our findings suggest that algorithmic instability may be a contributing factor to language models' poor zero-shot performance across certain logical reasoning tasks, as they struggle to abstract different problem-solving strategies and smoothly transition between them.

papers.title: Beyond Exponential Decay: Rethinking Error Accumulation in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) suffer from exponential decay in reliability with sequence length, and proposes an alternative framework based on key tokens, stratified manifolds, and self-consistency.
papers.core_contribution: The paper challenges the exponential decay hypothesis of LLM reliability and proposes a new theoretical framework based on key tokens, stratified manifolds, and self-consistency, explaining how LLMs maintain coherence over long sequences.
papers.conclusion: LLMs are more resilient than the exponential decay hypothesis suggests; by understanding and targeting the sparse key tokens and leveraging stratified manifolds and self-consistency, we can develop more efficient and reliable language systems.
papers.key_findings:
Only about 5-10% of tokens are 'key tokens' that critically influence global coherence and factual accuracy, while the majority are predictable non-key tokens.
LLM embeddings form stratified manifolds (semantic patches) that compartmentalize errors and provide natural error correction, preventing minor perturbations from causing semantic shifts.
Multiple reasoning paths tend to converge on correct answers while errors diverge, enabling ensemble methods like self-consistency to significantly mitigate errors.
The probability of a completely correct sequence scales with the number of key tokens (k) rather than total tokens (n), leading to much slower degradation (e.g., power-law or constant) than exponential decay.
Practical implications include focusing computational resources on key tokens, using targeted ensemble methods at uncertain decision points, and designing modular architectures aligned with semantic domains.
papers.limitation: The arguments draw primarily on existing studies and remain somewhat qualitative. Future research should develop more rigorous bounds based on attention mechanisms and state clustering, better quantify key token proportions across tasks, and bridge token-level and reasoning-step analyses.
future_direction: Develop more rigorous bounds based on attention mechanisms and state clustering.
Better quantify key token proportions across different tasks.
Bridge token-level and reasoning-step analyses.
papers.abstract: The prevailing assumption of an exponential decay in large language model (LLM) reliability with sequence length, predicated on independent per-token error probabilities, posits an inherent limitation for long autoregressive outputs. Our research fundamentally challenges this view by synthesizing emerging evidence that LLM errors are not uniformly distributed but are concentrated at sparse "key tokens" ($5-10\%$ of total tokens) representing critical decision junctions. By distinguishing these high-impact tokens from the increasingly predictable majority, we introduce a new reliability formula explaining the sustained coherence of modern LLMs over thousands of tokens. Converging research streams reveal that long-context performance primarily depends on accurately navigating a few crucial semantic decision points rather than on uniform token-level accuracy, enabling targeted strategies that significantly outperform brute-force approaches. We thus propose a framework for next-generation systems centered on selective preservation of semantically vital tokens, dynamic computational allocation at uncertain decision boundaries, multi-path exploration at ambiguities, and architectures aligned with natural semantic domains. This marks a fundamental shift from raw scaling to strategic reasoning, promising breakthrough performance without proportionate computational scaling and offering a more nuanced understanding that supersedes the exponential decay hypothesis, thereby opening pathways toward substantially more powerful and efficient language systems.

papers.title: Counting Hypothesis: Potential Mechanism of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do large language models support in-context learning? What is the underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the counting hypothesis, which suggests that LLMs support in-context learning by using context-dependent subspaces to encode potential answers and counting the strengths of contexts across examples.
papers.conclusion: The counting hypothesis offers a plausible explanation for ICL, where LLMs use context-dependent subspaces to encode answers and count contextual strengths across examples, supported by component analysis of residual streams.
papers.key_findings:
Residual streams of separator and answer tokens share common components, as shown by dictionary learning and ICA.
The last separator's residual stream aligns with answer token components, especially in deeper layers.
The coding coefficients of the last separator correlate with the minimum distance between answer and separator components.
The ratio R (based on coding coefficients of top components) differs significantly between correct and incorrect predictions, suggesting embedding components are associated with decision-making.
The counting hypothesis is supported by component analysis of residual streams.
papers.limitation:
The ideal case assumptions (e.g., invariance of example order) may not always hold in practice.
The component analysis methods (dictionary learning and ICA) may not be optimal for extracting the subspaces used by LLMs.
future_direction: Explore effective algorithms to investigate LLMs’ subspace associated with decision-making.
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) indicates that large language models (LLMs) pretrained on a massive amount of data can learn specific tasks from input prompts' examples. ICL is notable for two reasons. First, it does not need modification of LLMs' internal structure. Second, it enables LLMs to perform a wide range of tasks/functions with a few examples demonstrating a desirable task. ICL opens up new ways to utilize LLMs in more domains, but its underlying mechanisms still remain poorly understood, making error correction and diagnosis extremely challenging. Thus, it is imperative that we better understand the limitations of ICL and how exactly LLMs support ICL. Inspired by ICL properties and LLMs' functional modules, we propose 1the counting hypothesis' of ICL, which suggests that LLMs' encoding strategy may underlie ICL, and provide supporting evidence.

papers.title: On Memorization of Large Language Models in Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does memorization explain LLMs' performance on reasoning benchmarks, and is memorization only detrimental to learning to reason?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a memorization score (LiMem) and a dynamic K&K benchmark to show that fine-tuned LLMs memorize training puzzles but also improve in generalization, developing reasoning skills alongside memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that memorization and reasoning coexist in fine-tuned LLMs, and the proposed memorization score (LiMem) helps quantify the interplay between them.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can interpolate and memorize training puzzles after fine-tuning, achieving near-perfect accuracy, but struggle with slight variations.
Fine-tuning leads to heavy memorization but also consistently improves generalization performance on K&K puzzles.
LLMs develop reasoning skills on K&K puzzles alongside memorization, as shown by transferability across difficulty levels and probing internal representations.
Fine-tuning with detailed reasoning steps (CoT) can further boost generalization, even when fine-tuned with wrong reasoning steps.
Per-sample memorization score reveals how LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization when solving logical puzzles.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Knights and Knaves puzzles and may not generalize to other reasoning tasks.
The memorization score LiMem may not capture all forms of memorization.
future_direction: Extend the study to other reasoning tasks beyond K&K puzzles.
Investigate the effect of model scale on memorization and reasoning.
Improve the memorization score to better capture memorization behaviors.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve good performance on challenging reasoning benchmarks, yet could also make basic reasoning mistakes. This contrasting behavior is puzzling when it comes to understanding the mechanisms behind LLMs' reasoning capabilities. One hypothesis is that the increasingly high and nearly saturated performance on common reasoning benchmarks could be due to the memorization of similar problems. In this paper, we systematically investigate this hypothesis with a quantitative measurement of memorization in reasoning tasks, using a dynamically generated logical reasoning benchmark based on Knights and Knaves (K&K) puzzles. We found that LLMs could interpolate the training puzzles (achieving near-perfect accuracy) after fine-tuning, yet fail when those puzzles are slightly perturbed, suggesting that the models heavily rely on memorization to solve those training puzzles. On the other hand, we show that while fine-tuning leads to heavy memorization, it also consistently improves generalization performance. In-depth analyses with perturbation tests, cross difficulty-level transferability, probing model internals, and fine-tuning with wrong answers suggest that the LLMs learn to reason on K&K puzzles despite training data memorization. This phenomenon indicates that LLMs exhibit a complex interplay between memorization and genuine reasoning abilities. Finally, our analysis with per-sample memorization score sheds light on how LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization in solving logical puzzles. Our code and data are available at https://memkklogic.github.io.

papers.title: Information Anxiety in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of entity popularity on the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs, and do queries about popular entities cause ambiguity or confusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces 'information anxiety', a phenomenon where LLMs exhibit internal strains when processing highly popular queries, leading to rapid convergence of probability distributions but poor attention and inconsistent fact retrieval across lexical variations.
papers.conclusion: Information anxiety reveals vulnerabilities in LLMs' processing of prevalent information, emphasizing the need for robust evaluation and better pretraining data scrutiny.
papers.key_findings:
For highly popular questions, the predicted probability distribution converges earlier to the target distribution.
LLMs pay lower attention to constraint tokens in popular queries, indicating poor engagement with query details.
Retrieved facts across lexical variations become more dissimilar as query popularity increases, showing sensitivity to phrasing.
LLMs struggle to segregate facts from distinct relations for popular subjects, leading to higher inter-relation similarity.
Despite internal inconsistencies, LLMs remain confident in predictions for popular queries, as shown by high probability scores.
papers.limitation:
Entity and popularity formatted datasets like PopQA are hard to curate.
Developing better proxies for entity popularity in pretraining data is non-trivial.
Challenges in tracking and standardizing pretraining data quality due to volume and closed-source nature.
future_direction: Reducing sensitivity to lexical variations in knowledge queries.
Reducing popularity-dependent strains in internal mechanisms of LLMs.
Exploring alternative proxies for entity popularity in pretraining corpora.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance as knowledge repositories, enabling models to understand user queries and generate accurate and context-aware responses. Extensive evaluation setups have corroborated the positive correlation between the retrieval capability of LLMs and the frequency of entities in their pretraining corpus. We take the investigation further by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs. Our work focuses on three critical dimensions - the impact of entity popularity, the models' sensitivity to lexical variations in query formulation, and the progression of hidden state representations across LLM layers. Our preliminary findings reveal that popular questions facilitate early convergence of internal states toward the correct answer. However, as the popularity of a query increases, retrieved attributes across lexical variations become increasingly dissimilar and less accurate. Interestingly, we find that LLMs struggle to disentangle facts, grounded in distinct relations, from their parametric memory when dealing with highly popular subjects. Through a case study, we explore these latent strains within LLMs when processing highly popular queries, a phenomenon we term information anxiety. The emergence of information anxiety in LLMs underscores the adversarial injection in the form of linguistic variations and calls for a more holistic evaluation of frequently occurring entities.

papers.title: Give Me the Facts! A Survey on Factual Knowledge Probing in Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: What methods and datasets are used to probe pre-trained language models for factual knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: This paper surveys methods and datasets for factual knowledge probing in pre-trained language models, proposes a categorization scheme for probing methods based on adaptations to inputs, models, and outputs, and synthesizes insights about knowledge retention and prompt optimization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by discussing future work directions, including improving probing methods by combining adaptations across multiple dimensions, constructing unbiased and comprehensive datasets, and moving beyond simple correctness counts to more comprehensive evaluation schemes.
papers.key_findings:
Factual knowledge probing methods can be categorized based on how their inputs, outputs, and the probed PLMs are adapted.
A wide variety of datasets exist for factual probing, which can be categorized into general knowledge, domain-specific knowledge, and datasets targeting other aspects like consistency or updating knowledge.
Knowledge retention in PLMs is affected by factors such as model size, pre-training data, and the number of training epochs.
Prompt optimization can improve fact retrieval but may introduce biases, and the choice between using optimized or non-optimized prompts depends on the evaluation goal.
Several obstacles hinder the adoption of PLMs as knowledge bases, including issues with consistency, updating knowledge, and interpretability, though recent methods aim to address these.
papers.limitation:
The corpus construction relied on publications citing Petroni et al. (2019), potentially missing parallel works or works that do not directly cite this seminal paper.
The survey focuses on works about factual knowledge and excludes works on other types of knowledge (e.g., linguistic or commonsense), though methods for those types might be applicable to factual knowledge probing.
future_direction: Improving probing methods by introducing adaptations across two or more dimensions (e.g., optimizing inputs while also debiasing outputs).
Constructing unbiased and comprehensive probing datasets that correspond to the capacity of recently published large PLMs.

Developing comprehensive evaluation schemes that include factors like answer frequency, pre-training corpus creation period, model size, and training epochs, rather than just counting correct answers.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) are trained on vast unlabeled data, rich in world knowledge. This fact has sparked the interest of the community in quantifying the amount of factual knowledge present in PLMs, as this explains their performance on downstream tasks, and potentially justifies their use as knowledge bases. In this work, we survey methods and datasets that are used to probe PLMs for factual knowledge. Our contributions are: (1) We propose a categorization scheme for factual probing methods that is based on how their inputs, outputs and the probed PLMs are adapted; (2) We provide an overview of the datasets used for factual probing; (3) We synthesize insights about knowledge retention and prompt optimization in PLMs, analyze obstacles to adopting PLMs as knowledge bases and outline directions for future work.

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. This aligns with prior work showing that ICL is mediated by task vectors. We further demonstrate that these task vectors are well approximated by a sparse sum of SAE latents, including these task-execution features. To explore the ICL mechanism, we adapt the sparse feature circuits methodology of Marks et al. (2024) to work for the much larger Gemma-1 2B model, with 30 times as many parameters, and to the more complex task of ICL. Through circuit finding, we discover task-detecting features with corresponding SAE latents that activate earlier in the prompt, that detect when tasks have been performed. They are causally linked with task-execution features through the attention and MLP sublayers.

papers.title: Attention Deficits in Language Models: Causal Explanations for Procedural Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How can we decompose and formally diagnose procedural hallucinations in language models, where the model fails to use information it has computed?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for diagnosing procedural hallucinations in language models, decomposing errors into gating (Stage 2A) and binding (Stage 2B) failures, formalizes 'present but not used' via information theory, and shows checkpointing can restore long-context binding.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a rigorous framework for understanding procedural hallucinations, decomposing errors into gating and binding failures, formalizing routing efficiency via information theory, and providing bounds and diagnostics validated empirically.
papers.key_findings:
Stage 2B errors (wrong candidate selection) dominate procedural hallucinations in the hard regime.
On Stage 2B error trials, a linear probe on the final-layer residual stream recovers the correct value far above chance, indicating the information is present but not used.
Oracle checkpointing (restating the true binding near the query) can nearly eliminate Stage 2B failures at long distance.
Activation patching localizes routing failures to late MLP layers.
The framework formalizes 'present but not used' via available vs. used mutual information and provides pseudo-prior interventions for diagnosis.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic claims require activation access and thus apply directly only to open-weight models.
For hosted APIs, output-level and trace-level diagnostics are provided but I_avail cannot be estimated without activations.
Trace auditing detects certificate failures but does not prove faithfulness to the model's hidden chain-of-thought.
Experiments focus on synthetic binding tasks; validation on naturalistic long-context tasks remains open.
future_direction: Validation of the framework on naturalistic long-context tasks such as document QA.
Investigating whether architectural solutions to improve routing efficiency can be trained or induced.
papers.abstract: Large language models can follow complex procedures yet fail at a seemingly trivial final step: reporting a value they themselves computed moments earlier. We study this phenomenon as \emph{procedural hallucination}: failure to execute a verifiable, prompt-grounded specification even when the correct value is present in context. In long-context binding tasks with a known single-token candidate set, we find that many errors are readout-stage routing failures. Specifically, failures decompose into Stage~2A (gating) errors, where the model does not enter answer mode, and Stage~2B (binding) errors, where it enters answer mode but selects the wrong candidate (often due to recency bias). In the hard regime, Stage~2B accounts for most errors across model families in our tasks (Table~1). On Stage~2B error trials, a linear probe on the final-layer residual stream recovers the correct value far above chance (e.g., 74\% vs.\ 2\% on Qwen2.5-3B; Table~2), indicating that the answer is encoded but not used. We formalize ``present but not used'' via available vs.\ used mutual information and pseudo-prior interventions, yielding output-computable diagnostics and information-budget certificates. Finally, an oracle checkpointing intervention that restates the true binding near the query can nearly eliminate Stage~2B failures at long distance (e.g., Qwen2.5-3B $0/400 \rightarrow 399/400$ at $k = 1024$; Table~8).

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: REMA: A Unified Reasoning Manifold Framework for Interpreting Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we understand and localize reasoning failures in Large Language Models by analyzing the geometric structure of their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of the 'Reasoning Manifold' and the REMA framework, which diagnoses reasoning failures by quantifying and localizing the geometric deviation of erroneous internal representations from the manifold formed by correct ones.
papers.conclusion: REMA provides a novel geometric perspective for interpreting LLM reasoning, demonstrating that deviations from a 'Reasoning Manifold' are indicative of errors and allowing for the localization of failure points within the model's inference path.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states of both correct and incorrect reasoning exhibit low-dimensional structures (low Intrinsic Dimension).
Representations of erroneous reasoning consistently show statistically significant geometric deviation from the manifold of correct reasoning.
These deviations can be traced back to specific model layers (divergence points), revealing model- and task-dependent patterns of failure origins.
The relative deviation distance is negatively correlated with model accuracy, suggesting more difficult tasks lead to larger deviations.
Correct and error reasoning representations are highly separable in the latent space, as shown by UMAP/t-SNE visualizations and classifier accuracy.
papers.limitation:
The manifold approximation depends on the diversity and density of the correct samples.
Binary partitioning of samples into 'correct' and 'error' based on exact text match might misclassify 'nearly correct' reasoning.
future_direction: Building more precise manifold models using advanced manifold learning techniques.
Investigating the fundamental reasons for the formation of reasoning manifolds.
Exploring more fine-grained, confidence-based, or soft-scoring-based partitioning methods.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform complex reasoning and their failure mechanisms is a challenge in interpretability research. To provide a measurable geometric analysis perspective, we define the concept of the Reasoning Manifold, a latent low-dimensional geometric structure formed by the internal representations corresponding to all correctly reasoned generations. This structure can be conceptualized as the embodiment of the effective thinking paths that the model has learned to successfully solve a given task. Based on this concept, we build REMA, a framework that explains the origins of failures by quantitatively comparing the spatial relationships of internal model representations corresponding to both erroneous and correct reasoning samples. Specifically, REMA first quantifies the geometric deviation of each erroneous representation by calculating its k-nearest neighbors distance to the approximated manifold formed by correct representations, thereby providing a unified failure signal. It then localizes the divergence points where these deviations first become significant by tracking this deviation metric across the model's layers and comparing it against a baseline of internal fluctuations from correct representations, thus identifying where the reasoning chain begins to go off-track. Our extensive experiments on diverse language and multimodal models and tasks demonstrate the low-dimensional nature of the reasoning manifold and the high separability between erroneous and correct reasoning representations. The results also validate the effectiveness of the REMA framework in analyzing the origins of reasoning failures. This research connects abstract reasoning failures to measurable geometric deviations in representations, providing new avenues for in-depth understanding and diagnosis of the internal computational processes of black-box models.

papers.title: Is Grokking Worthwhile? Functional Analysis and Transferability of Generalization Circuits in Transformers
papers.research_question: Is a grokked model superior to its non-grokked counterparts on downstream tasks? Furthermore, is the extensive computational cost of waiting for the grokking phase worthwhile?
papers.core_contribution: Grokking does not represent genuine acquisition of generalized reasoning; instead, it integrates memorized facts into naturally established circuits, and grokked transformers show limited transferability to novel facts.
papers.conclusion: Grokking merely integrates memorized facts into naturally established circuits, and grokked transformers have limited transferability to novel facts, suggesting a trade-off between data scarcity and computational resources.
papers.key_findings:
Non-grokked and grokked models follow identical reasoning paths on in-distribution compositional queries, indicating that grokking is the process of integrating memorized atomic facts into an established reasoning structure.
Grokking and the formation of a Generalization Circuit are not intrinsically linked; behavioral grokking can occur without circuit formation.
Generalization Circuits exhibit limited transferability; they do not imply full mastery of compositional logic and struggle with new facts in certain positions.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints limit exhaustive exploration of fake grokking due to prolonged training cycles.
Findings are constrained to parameter-sharing Transformer architectures and may not extend to standard transformers.
future_direction: Systematically categorize which data distributions favor circuit formation over pattern memorization.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at factual retrieval, they often struggle with the "curse of two-hop reasoning" in compositional tasks. Recent research suggests that parameter-sharing transformers can bridge this gap by forming a "Generalization Circuit" during a prolonged "grokking" phase. A fundamental question arises: Is a grokked model superior to its non-grokked counterparts on downstream tasks? Furthermore, is the extensive computational cost of waiting for the grokking phase worthwhile? In this work, we conduct a mechanistic study to evaluate the Generalization Circuit's role in knowledge assimilation and transfer. We demonstrate that: (i) The inference paths established by non-grokked and grokked models for in-distribution compositional queries are identical. This suggests that the "Generalization Circuit" does not represent the sudden acquisition of a new reasoning paradigm. Instead, we argue that grokking is the process of integrating memorized atomic facts into an naturally established reasoning path. (ii) Achieving high accuracy on unseen cases after prolonged training and the formation of a certain reasoning path are not bound; they can occur independently under specific data regimes. (iii) Even a mature circuit exhibits limited transferability when integrating new knowledge, suggesting that "grokked" Transformers do not achieve a full mastery of compositional logic.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks.
